<a id="dy-6"></a>
## Layer 6: Families, specialization and orbit intersections

Power and Lattès maps test the earlier layers. Family heights and specialization feed critical-height and Legendre estimates. The embedding route constructs arbitrary-field integral presentations and transports a primitive root before producing the p-adic model for étale DML. Hybrid, activity, classification and representative-height suppliers keep their open proof leaves.

Planets: Lattès map; Call–Silverman specialization theorem; Critical height; Critical height is a moduli height; Uniform common torsion images for Legendre pairs; Étale dynamical Mordell–Lang.

<a id="target-arithmeticdynamics-dy-6-power-map"></a>

### 6.1 The power map z ↦ z^d on the projective line

Let K be a field and d ≥ 1 an integer. The power map P_d : ℙ¹_K → ℙ¹_K is the rational map (DY.0/rational-map-of-the-projective-line) given by the pair of homogeneous forms (X^d, Y^d): [x : y] ↦ [x^d : y^d]. In the affine coordinate z = x/y it is z ↦ z^d, with P_d(0) = 0 and P_d(∞) = ∞ (∞ = [1 : 0]). It has degree d, and Res(X^d, Y^d) = 1 in the normalisation of DY.0/resultant-of-a-rational-map. Iterates P_dⁿ are composites of morphisms.

K is any field; the definition needs no characteristic hypothesis. d ≥ 1; the dynamical statements (canonical height, preperiodic points, multipliers) assume d ≥ 2, where P_d is polarised: P_d^*O(1) ≅ O(d). The multiplier d at a fixed root of unity and the critical-point count use char K ∤ d (in characteristic p | d, P_d is inseparable and every affine point is critical).

X^d and Y^d are homogeneous of degree d; over an algebraic closure their only common zero is (0, 0), since x^d = y^d = 0 forces x = y = 0. Hence (X^d, Y^d) is a DY.0 rational map of degree d. Resultant: dehomogenising, Res(X^d, 1) = 1 (Mathlib Polynomial.resultant; the Sylvester matrix of (X^d, 1) is the identity), so Res(X^d, Y^d) = 1 and P_d has good reduction at every nonarchimedean place (DY.0/good-reduction-of-a-rational-map). Composition: (X^d, Y^d) ∘ (X^e, Y^e) = ((X^e)^d, (Y^e)^d) = (X^{de}, Y^{de}) as forms, so P_d ∘ P_e = P_{de} as rational maps and P_dⁿ = P_{dⁿ} by induction on n. Fixed points: [x : y] with x^d y = x y^d, i.e. xy(x^{d−1} − y^{d−1}) = 0: the points 0, ∞ and the (d−1)-th roots of unity. The derivative of z^d at a fixed point ζ with ζ^{d−1} = 1 is dζ^{d−1} = d, at 0 it is 0 (d ≥ 2), and at ∞ the conjugate map w ↦ w^d gives 0.

*Needs:* [`ArithmeticDynamics:DY.0/rational-map-of-the-projective-line`](#target-arithmeticdynamics-dy-0-rational-map-of-the-projective-line); [`ArithmeticDynamics:DY.0/resultant-of-a-rational-map`](#target-arithmeticdynamics-dy-0-resultant-of-a-rational-map); [`ArithmeticDynamics:DY.0/good-reduction-of-a-rational-map`](#target-arithmeticdynamics-dy-0-good-reduction-of-a-rational-map); `mathlib:Polynomial.resultant`; `mathlib:Polynomial.natDegree_X_pow`; `mathlib:Polynomial.resultant_eq_zero_iff`.

The reusable interface consists of the following statements.

- **`powerMap_apply`** (simp): P_d(z) = z^d for z in K and P_d(∞) = ∞.
- **`powerMap_comp`** (relation): P_d ∘ P_e = P_{de} as rational maps.
- **`powerMap_iterate`** (relation): P_dⁿ = P_{dⁿ} as rational maps.
- **`powerMap_degree`** (characterisation): The degree of P_d is d.
- **`powerMap_resultant`** (other): Res(X^d, Y^d) = 1; hence P_d has good reduction at every nonarchimedean place (DY.0/good-reduction-of-a-rational-map).
- **`powerMap_conj_inv`** (relation): P_d commutes with ι(z) = 1/z and with z ↦ ζz for every (d−1)-th root of unity ζ.
- **`powerMap_isFixedPt_iff`** (characterisation): For d ≥ 2, the fixed points of P_d are 0, ∞ and the (d−1)-th roots of unity.
- **`powerMap_multiplier`** (other): For d ≥ 2 the multiplier (DY.2/multiplier-of-a-periodic-cycle) of the fixed points 0 and ∞ is 0; if char K ∤ d, the multiplier of a fixed (d−1)-th root of unity is d, and the n-cycle of a root of unity of exact period n has multiplier dⁿ.
- **`powerMap_map`** (functoriality): For a field homomorphism σ : K → L, the base change of P_d over K is P_d over L.

**Checks.**

- **`powerMap_two_iterate_three`** (computation): Over ℚ, P_2³(2) = 256 and P_2³(∞) = ∞.
- **`powerMap_one`** (degenerate): P_1 is the identity rational map of ℙ¹.
- **`powerMap_canonicalHeight_eq`** (compatibility): For d ≥ 2 and x ∈ ℚ̄, the canonical height ĥ_{P_d}(x) equals the absolute Weil height NumberField.absLogHeight₁ x (ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.6/canonical-height-power-map, from Height.logHeight₁_pow).
- **`powerMap_two_not_preperiodic`** (non-example): The point 2 ∈ ℚ is not preperiodic for P_2 (its orbit 2, 4, 16, 256, … is injective), whereas every root of unity is.

**Endpoint checks.** P_2 over ℚ: P_2(2) = 4, P_2³(2) = 256, P_2(∞) = ∞, P_2(−1) = 1. P_d ∘ P_e = P_{de} holds as an equality of rational maps (of forms up to scaling), not only on points. Res(X^d, Y^d) = 1, so P_d has good reduction at every finite place of every number field.

<a id="target-arithmeticdynamics-dy-6-lattes-map"></a>

### 6.2 The Lattès map of multiplication by n on a Weierstrass curve

Let F be a field, E a Weierstrass curve over F (Mathlib WeierstrassCurve) with discriminant Δ(E) ≠ 0, and n ∈ ℤ with n ≠ 0. The Lattès map f_{E,n} : ℙ¹_F → ℙ¹_F is the rational map (DY.0/rational-map-of-the-projective-line) given by the forms (Φ_n^h(X, Z), ΨSq_n^h(X, Z)), the homogenisations in degree n² (Mathlib Polynomial.homogenize) of Mathlib's division polynomials WeierstrassCurve.Φ n and WeierstrassCurve.ΨSq n. In the affine coordinate x it is x ↦ Φ_n(x)/ΨSq_n(x), with f_{E,n}(x) = ∞ when ΨSq_n(x) = 0 and f_{E,n}(∞) = ∞. It is the descent of [n] : E → E through the x-coordinate x : E → ℙ¹ (the quotient by P ↦ −P, with x(O) = ∞): f_{E,n} ∘ x = x ∘ [n] (DY.6/lattes-map-semiconjugacy). For |n| ≥ 2 it has degree n².

F any field; E any Weierstrass curve over F with Δ(E) ≠ 0 (no characteristic hypothesis: the coprimality of Φ_n and ΨSq_n holds in every characteristic). n ≠ 0 (ΨSq_0 = 0); f_{E,±1} is the identity and the dynamical statements assume |n| ≥ 2. Δ(E) ≠ 0 is necessary: for the cuspidal cubic y² = x³ the forms Φ_2 = X⁴ and ΨSq_2 = 4X³ share the root 0.

Degrees: Φ_n has degree n² and leading coefficient 1 (WeierstrassCurve.natDegree_Φ, WeierstrassCurve.leadingCoeff_Φ) and ΨSq_n has degree at most n² − 1 (WeierstrassCurve.natDegree_ΨSq_le); ΨSq_n ≠ 0 (WeierstrassCurve.ΨSq_ne_zero_of_Δ_ne_zero). Φ_n and ΨSq_n are coprime (WeierstrassCurve.isCoprime_Φ_ΨSq, using Δ ≠ 0), so the degree-n² homogenisations have no common zero on ℙ¹ over an algebraic closure: at Z ≠ 0 by coprimality, at [1 : 0] because Φ_n^h(1, 0) = 1. They therefore define a DY.0 rational map of degree n². f_{E,n}(∞) = [Φ_n^h(1, 0) : ΨSq_n^h(1, 0)] = [1 : 0] since deg ΨSq_n < n². n = 2: Φ_2 = X⁴ − b₄X² − 2b₆X − b₈ and ΨSq_2 = Ψ₂Sq = 4X³ + b₂X² + 2b₄X + b₆ (WeierstrassCurve.Φ_two, WeierstrassCurve.ΨSq_two, WeierstrassCurve.Ψ₂Sq); their resultant is Δ(E)² (a direct computation), so f_{E,2} has good reduction at every place of good reduction of E away from 2.

*Needs:* `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.Φ`; `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.ΨSq`; `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.Ψ₂Sq`; `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.natDegree_Φ`; `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.leadingCoeff_Φ`; `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.natDegree_ΨSq_le`; `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.Φ_two`; `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.ΨSq_two`; `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.Φ_neg`; `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.ΨSq_neg`; `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.map_Φ`; `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.map_ΨSq`; `mathlib:Polynomial.homogenize`; `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.Δ`; `tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.isCoprime_Φ_ΨSq`; `tauceti:WeierstrassCurve.ΨSq_ne_zero_of_Δ_ne_zero`; [`ArithmeticDynamics:DY.0/rational-map-of-the-projective-line`](#target-arithmeticdynamics-dy-0-rational-map-of-the-projective-line).

The reusable interface consists of the following statements.

- **`lattesMap_apply`** (simp): For x in F: f_{E,n}(x) = Φ_n(x)/ΨSq_n(x) if ΨSq_n(x) ≠ 0 and f_{E,n}(x) = ∞ otherwise; f_{E,n}(∞) = ∞.

- **`lattesMap_neg`** (relation): f_{E,−n} = f_{E,n} (WeierstrassCurve.Φ_neg, WeierstrassCurve.ΨSq_neg).
- **`lattesMap_one`** (simp): f_{E,1} = id.
- **`lattesMap_two`** (simp): f_{E,2}(x) = (x⁴ − b₄x² − 2b₆x − b₈)/(4x³ + b₂x² + 2b₄x + b₆).
- **`lattesMap_resultant_two`** (other): The resultant of (Φ_2, ΨSq_2) is Δ(E)², so f_{E,2} has good reduction (DY.0/good-reduction-of-a-rational-map) at every nonarchimedean place v ∤ 2 at which E has good reduction.
- **`lattesMap_map`** (functoriality): For a field homomorphism σ : F → L, f_{σ(E),n} = σ(f_{E,n}) (WeierstrassCurve.map_Φ, WeierstrassCurve.map_ΨSq).
- **`lattesMap_iterate`** (relation): f_{E,n}^k = f_{E,n^k} as rational maps (from DY.6/lattes-map-comp).
- **`lattesMap_isFixedPt_infty`** (simp): ∞ is a fixed point of f_{E,n}.

**Checks.**

- **`lattesMap_two_y2_eq_x3_sub_x`** (computation): For E : y² = x³ − x over ℚ, f_{E,2}(x) = (x² + 1)²/(4x(x² − 1)); in particular f_{E,2}(2) = 25/24.
- **`lattesMap_one_eq_id`** (degenerate): f_{E,1} and f_{E,−1} are the identity rational map.
- **`lattesMap_apply_xCoord`** (compatibility): For P = (x₀, y₀) ∈ E(F) with nP = (x₁, y₁) affine, f_{E,n}(x₀) = x₁ = x₁ · ΨSq_n(x₀)/ΨSq_n(x₀), matching Tau Ceti WeierstrassCurve.mul_eval_ΨSq_eq_eval_Φ_of_zsmul.
- **`lattesMap_not_of_singular`** (non-example): For the singular cubic y² = x³ over ℚ (Δ = 0), Φ_2 = X⁴ and ΨSq_2 = 4X³ are not coprime, so the pair does not define a degree-4 map (it reduces to x ↦ x/4).

**Endpoint checks.** E : y² = x³ − x over ℚ: f_{E,2}(x) = (x² + 1)²/(4x(x² − 1)), with f_{E,2}(0) = f_{E,2}(±1) = ∞ (the 2-torsion) and f_{E,2}(∞) = ∞. The Legendre curve E_t: f_{E_t,2} = (x² − t)²/(4x(x − 1)(x − t)), the map (2.1) of DeMarco–Krieger–Ye (DY.6/legendre-lattes-map). deg f_{E,3} = 9: Φ_3 has degree 9 and ΨSq_3 = Ψ₃² has degree 8 in characteristic zero; that denominator degree may drop in positive characteristic.

<a id="target-arithmeticdynamics-dy-6-two-torsion-translation"></a>

### 6.3 Translation by a 2-torsion point acts on the x-line by a Möbius involution

Let F be a field of characteristic ≠ 2, E/F a Weierstrass curve with Δ(E) ≠ 0 and T = (e, y_T) ∈ E(F) a point of order 2 (so Ψ₂Sq(e) = 0 and y_T = −(a₁e + a₃)/2). Let τ_T be the Möbius transformation τ_T(x) = e + Ψ₂Sq′(e)/(4(x − e)), with τ_T(e) = ∞ and τ_T(∞) = e, where Ψ₂Sq′(e) = 12e² + 2b₂e + 2b₄ ≠ 0. Then x(P + T) = τ_T(x(P)) for every P ∈ E(F), and τ_T ∘ τ_T = id. For T = O set τ_O = id.

char F ≠ 2; Δ(E) ≠ 0 (so e is a simple root of Ψ₂Sq and Ψ₂Sq′(e) ≠ 0); T of exact order 2.

2T = O means y_T = negY(e, y_T), i.e. 2y_T + a₁e + a₃ = 0, and substituting in the curve equation gives Ψ₂Sq(e) = 0 (Ψ₂Sq = (2y + a₁x + a₃)² on the curve). For P = (x, y) with x ≠ e, Mathlib's addition formula (WeierstrassCurve.Affine.Point.add_of_X_ne, WeierstrassCurve.Affine.addX, WeierstrassCurve.Affine.slope) gives x(P + T) = λ² + a₁λ − a₂ − x − e with λ = (y − y_T)/(x − e); reducing modulo the curve equation (a polynomial identity checked symbolically) gives e + Ψ₂Sq′(e)/(4(x − e)). P = T gives O (x = ∞ = τ_T(e)); P = O gives T (τ_T(∞) = e); P = −P′ with x(P′) = e only for P′ = T. Ψ₂Sq′(e) ≠ 0 because a double root of Ψ₂Sq would make Δ = 0 (Ψ₂Sq has discriminant 16Δ); τ_T is an involution because translation by T is.

*Needs:* `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.Point.add_of_X_ne`; `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.addX`; `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.slope`; `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.Affine.negY`; `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.Ψ₂Sq`; `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.b₂`; `mathlib:WeierstrassCurve.b₄`; [`ArithmeticDynamics:DY.0/conjugacy-of-rational-maps`](#target-arithmeticdynamics-dy-0-conjugacy-of-rational-maps).

**Endpoint checks.** Legendre curve E_t, T = (0, 0): τ_T(x) = t/x (Ψ₂Sq = 4x(x − 1)(x − t), Ψ₂Sq′(0) = 4t). E : y² = x³ − x, T = (1, 0): τ_T(x) = 1 + 2/(x − 1) = (x + 1)/(x − 1).

### 6.4 Postcritically finite rational maps

Let K be a field of characteristic 0 and f a rational map of degree d ≥ 2 over K. The postcritical set of f is PC(f) = ⋃_{n ≥ 1} fⁿ(supp Crit(f)) ⊆ ℙ¹(K̄). The map f is postcritically finite (PCF) if every critical point of f is preperiodic, equivalently if PC(f) is finite.

char K = 0; d ≥ 2.

supp Crit(f) is finite (DY.0/critical-points-of-a-rational-map), so PC(f) is finite iff every critical orbit is finite iff every critical point is preperiodic.

*Needs:* [`ArithmeticDynamics:DY.0/critical-points-of-a-rational-map`](#target-arithmeticdynamics-dy-0-critical-points-of-a-rational-map); `mathlib:Set.Finite`; `mathlib:Function.IsPeriodicPt`.

([demarco-mavraki-ye-2026](#source-parent-demarco-mavraki-ye-2026), §2.2, p. 8 (arXiv v3) — The definition of the node; [bijmst18](#source-parent-bijmst18), §11, p. 24 (arXiv v2) — Critical points as the points where f is not locally injective (local degree ≥ 2), and postcritical finiteness.)

The reusable interface consists of the following statements.

- **`postcriticalSet`** (data): PC(f) = ⋃_{n ≥ 1} fⁿ(supp Crit(f)).
- **`IsPostcriticallyFinite`** (data): Every critical point of f is preperiodic.
- **`isPostcriticallyFinite_iff_finite`** (characterisation): f is PCF iff PC(f) is finite.
- **`IsPostcriticallyFinite.conj`** (relation): PCF is invariant under conjugation by PGL₂(K̄).
- **`isPostcriticallyFinite_iterate_iff`** (relation): f is PCF iff fⁿ is PCF (n ≥ 1), by DY.0/critical-points-of-a-rational-map criticalPoints_iterate.
- **`IsPostcriticallyFinite.map`** (functoriality): PCF is preserved by field embeddings.

**Checks.**

- **`isPCF_sq_sub_two`** (computation): z² − 2 over ℚ is postcritically finite, with PC = {−2, 2, ∞}.
- **`isPCF_powerMap`** (degenerate): P_d (d ≥ 2) is PCF: its critical points 0 and ∞ are fixed, and PC(P_d) = {0, ∞}.
- **`isPCF_legendreLattesMap`** (compatibility): The Legendre maps f_t are PCF with PC(f_t) = {0, 1, t, ∞} (DY.6/lattes-map-postcritically-finite).
- **`not_isPCF_sq_add_one`** (non-example): z² + 1 over ℚ is not PCF: the orbit 0, 1, 2, 5, 26, … of the critical point 0 is infinite.

**Endpoint checks.** z² − 2 is PCF: 0 ↦ −2 ↦ 2 ↦ 2. z² + i is PCF: 0 ↦ i ↦ i − 1 ↦ −i ↦ i − 1. z² + 1 is not PCF: 0 ↦ 1 ↦ 2 ↦ 5 ↦ 26 ↦ ….

Consumers: DeMarco–Mavraki–Ye §1, §2.2 — PCF maps are the special points of M_d; the PCF points of M_d(ℚ̄) are the zeros of the critical height; Ingram, property C′ — ĥ_crit(f) = 0 iff f is PCF (DY.6/critical-height-eq-zero-iff-postcritically-finite); Benedetto et al., Conjecture 11.5–11.6 — the dynamical André–Oort conjecture concerns families with infinitely many PCF parameters (DY.6/dynamical-andre-oort-conjecture).

<a id="target-arithmeticdynamics-dy-6-rational-function-field-heights"></a>

### 6.5 Admissible absolute values and heights on a rational function field

Let k be a field and k(t) = RatFunc k. For each monic irreducible π ∈ k[t] let |g|_π := exp(−deg π · ord_π g), and let |g|_∞ := exp(deg num(g) − deg denom(g)) (Mathlib RatFunc.inftyValuation), for g ≠ 0. These are nonarchimedean absolute values; for g ≠ 0 almost all of them equal 1 at g; and ∏_v |g|_v = 1. They form an instance of Mathlib's Height.AdmissibleAbsValues on k(t) with no archimedean absolute values. The resulting logarithmic height is the degree height: Height.logHeight₁ g = max(deg num g, deg denom g), and for coprime p, q ∈ k[t] not both zero the height of [p : q] ∈ ℙ¹(k(t)) is Height.logHeight ![p, q] = max(deg p, deg q) =: h_{k(t)}([p : q]).

k any field (finite or infinite, any characteristic). The absolute values are normalised so that log|t|_∞ = 1: this is the height relative to the divisor (∞) of degree 1 on ℙ¹_k.

Each |·|_π and |·|_∞ comes from a discrete valuation (IsDedekindDomain.HeightOneSpectrum.valuation on k[t], RatFunc.inftyValuation) composed with x ↦ exp(−c·x); ultrametric, hence nonarchimedean. Finiteness of support: g ≠ 0 has finitely many zeros and poles among the monic irreducibles. Product formula: Σ_π deg π · ord_π(g) = deg num(g) − deg denom(g) by unique factorisation in k[t], which is −log|g|_∞. Height: Σ_v log⁺|g|_v = Σ_π deg π · max(0, −ord_π g) + max(0, deg num g − deg denom g) = deg denom g + max(0, deg num g − deg denom g) = max(deg num g, deg denom g); the vector formula follows in the same way with max over coordinates.

*Needs:* `mathlib:Height.AdmissibleAbsValues`; `mathlib:Height.logHeight₁`; `mathlib:Height.logHeight`; `mathlib:RatFunc.inftyValuation`; `mathlib:IsDedekindDomain.HeightOneSpectrum.valuation`; `mathlib:RatFunc.num`; `mathlib:RatFunc.denom`; `mathlib:RatFunc.intDegree`; `mathlib:RatFunc.finrank_eq_max_natDegree`; `mathlib:AbsoluteValue`.

([call-silverman-1993](#source-parent-call-silverman-1993), §4, p. 183 — For T = ℙ¹ these are the places of k(t)/k: the monic irreducible polynomials and ∞, with the degree height; [call-silverman-1993](#source-parent-call-silverman-1993), §1, p. 166 — Mathlib's Height.AdmissibleAbsValues is this notion; the node supplies the one-variable function field instance and the canonical height over any such field.)

<a id="target-arithmeticdynamics-dy-6-specialization-of-rational-maps"></a>

### 6.6 Specialisation of a one-parameter family of rational maps and of its points

Let k be a field with algebraic closure k̄ and f a rational map of ℙ¹ of degree d ≥ 1 over k(t) (DY.0/rational-map-of-the-projective-line). Choose forms F, G ∈ k[t][X, Y] of degree d representing f whose coefficients have no common factor in k[t] (a primitive representative; unique up to k^×). For t₀ ∈ k̄ let F_{t₀}, G_{t₀} ∈ k̄[X, Y] be obtained by evaluating the coefficients at t₀. The good set is T⁰(f) := {t₀ ∈ k̄ : Res(F, G)(t₀) ≠ 0}, where Res(F, G) ∈ k[t] (DY.0/resultant-of-a-rational-map); it is cofinite. For t₀ ∈ T⁰(f) the specialisation f_{t₀} := [F_{t₀} : G_{t₀}] is a rational map of degree d over k(t₀). For P ∈ ℙ¹(k(t)) written P = [p : q] with p, q ∈ k[t] coprime, its specialisation is P_{t₀} := [p(t₀) : q(t₀)] ∈ ℙ¹(k(t₀)), defined for every t₀ ∈ k̄.

k any field; the family is a map over the rational function field k(t) (base curve the t-line). Specialisation of maps is defined on T⁰(f); specialisation of points is defined everywhere since p and q have no common root.

Primitive representatives exist and are unique up to k^×: clear denominators and divide by the gcd of the coefficients (k[t] is a UFD). Res(F, G) ∈ k[t] is nonzero because F, G have no common zero over the algebraic closure of k(t); resultants commute with the evaluation map k[t] → k̄ (the Sylvester determinant is a polynomial in the coefficients), so Res(F_{t₀}, G_{t₀}) = Res(F, G)(t₀) and f_{t₀} has degree d exactly on T⁰(f). T⁰(f) is cofinite: its complement is the set of roots of the nonzero polynomial Res(F, G). For independence of representatives, write a second pair as a rational-function scalar times the primitive pair. At a good parameter, the primitive pair has at least one unit coefficient in the local DVR. If the second pair has a nonzero specialization, its scalar has valuation zero, so the specialized pairs differ by a nonzero scalar. Multiplying both forms by t−t₀ gives a zero pair and is excluded.

### 6.7 The constant of Mathlib's height bound under extension of number fields

Let K ⊆ L be number fields and p a finite family of polynomials with coefficients in K. Then Height.mulHeightBound computed over L of the image of p is at most (max(Height.mulHeightBound p over K, 1))^{[L:K]}. Consequently c(p) := log max(mulHeightBound_K(p), 1)/[K : ℚ] satisfies log max(mulHeightBound_L(p), 1) ≤ [L : ℚ] · c(p) for every finite extension L of K.

K ⊆ L number fields with Mathlib NumberField.instAdmissibleAbsValues on each.

Unfold Height.mulHeightBound: a product over the archimedean absolute values (with multiplicities) of sup_j Σ |coeff|_v and over the finite places of sup_j max(sup |coeff|_v, 1) (Height.mulHeightBound_eq). Each place w of L restricts to a place v of K, |c|_w = |c|_v^{[L_w:K_v]/…} for c ∈ K in the normalisation of Mathlib's places, and Σ_{w | v} [L_w : K_v] = [L : K]; group the factors of the L-product by the place of K below (NumberField.prod_archAbsVal_eq, NumberField.prod_nonarchAbsVal_eq), exactly as in DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.0/mul-height-algebra-map. Each group contributes at most the K-factor raised to [L : K] (archimedean sums: |Σ|-values are those of the embedding restricted to K, repeated [L : K] times in total), giving the inequality; divide logarithms by [L : ℚ] = [L : K][K : ℚ].

### 6.8 The critical height of a rational map

Let f be a rational map of ℙ¹ of degree d ≥ 2 defined over ℚ̄ (over a number field). The critical height is ĥ_crit(f) := Σ_{c} m_c · ĥ_f(c), summing over the critical points c of f (DY.0/critical-points-of-a-rational-map) with their multiplicities m_c, where ĥ_f is the absolute canonical height of DY.1/canonical-height-on-the-projective-line. It is a nonnegative real number, invariant under conjugation (DY.6/critical-height-conjugation-invariant), so it defines a function ĥ_crit : M_d(ℚ̄) → [0, ∞) on the moduli space of DY.0/moduli-space-of-rational-maps.

f defined over ℚ̄ (the canonical height of DY.1 is defined for maps over number fields); d ≥ 2.

The critical points lie in ℙ¹(ℚ̄) (roots of J(F, G), a nonzero form with algebraic coefficients); the sum is finite with 2d − 2 terms (DY.0/critical-points-of-a-rational-map). Nonnegativity from ĥ_f ≥ 0 (DY.1/canonical-height-on-the-projective-line). Descent to M_d(ℚ̄): DY.6/critical-height-conjugation-invariant.

### 6.9 Quantitative branch point near a small attracting multiplier

Let f(z)=λz·∏_{i=1}^{d−1}(1−α_i z)/∏_{j=1}^{d−1}(1−β_j z) have degree d≥2, fixing 0 and infinity, and M=max{|α_i|,|β_j|}>0. Over C set C_v=3^{d−1}, ε_v=min(1/8,1/C_v); over a complete algebraically closed nonarchimedean field of characteristic 0 or p>d set C_v=1, ε_v=min_{1≤m≤d}|m|^d. If 0<|λ|<ε_v, there is a nonzero branch value β with 0<|f^k(β)|M≤(C_v|λ|)^k for all k≥1.

The archimedean absolute value is the usual complex modulus. In the nonarchimedean case the field characteristic is 0 or p>d, as in Ingram §1; the residue characteristic can be at most d. A branch value is the image of a critical point, not necessarily the critical point itself.

Rescale so M=1. On the half-unit disc over C, or the open unit disc nonarchimedean, the displayed factorization bounds iterates by a geometric power and excludes hitting 0. Over C, if the relevant disc has no branch value, the inverse component maps unbranched to it. Koebe quarter bounds its conformal radius by 4 because a pole or nonzero root lies on the unit circle, whereas the multiplier gives radius 1/(2|λ|), a contradiction. Nonarchimedean: the Benedetto–Ingram–Jones–Levy theorem used in Ingram Lemma 8 yields a branch value in the unit disc if |λ| is below every directional multiplicity to the dth power. Those multiplicities lie between 1 and d, giving the stated ε_v. These two analytic suppliers remain explicit gaps.

### 6.12 Uniform hybrid escape potentials for meromorphic families

Let f_t be a degree-d≥2 meromorphic family of morphisms of P¹ on a punctured disc, with meromorphic homogeneous lift F_t having no common zero for t≠0. Fix 0<r<1 inside the parameter disc and the hybrid central norm |T|=r. With the Fubini–Study reference metric define u_n([z],t)=d^{-n} log(max_i |(F_t^n(z))_i| / ||z||₂^{d^n}), where F_t^n is the homogeneous compositional iterate. The finite-level hybrid extensions of (log r/log|t|)u_n converge uniformly over the closed hybrid disc |t|≤r to a continuous potential. Its central restriction is g_F([z])=lim_n d^{-n}log||F^n(z)||_sup−log||z||_sup over C((T)) with |T|=r, relative to the standard nonarchimedean model metric. Replacing F_t by h(t)F_t changes the limit by (log r/log|t|)log|h(t)|/(d−1) on complex fibres and by log|h|_r/(d−1) centrally.

The resultant may vanish at t=0 but not for t≠0; the family is meromorphic across 0. Use the Fubini–Study metric on complex O(1) and the standard model metric centrally. Scalar changes of the homogeneous lift use the displayed correction; continuity is stronger information than weak convergence of measures.

Coefficient meromorphy gives an upper bound by a power of |t|; a Nullstellensatz/resultant identity gives the lower bound by another power. Thus |u_{n+1}−u_n|≤C d^{-n}log|t|^{-1} (Favre Proposition 4.4). The hybrid scaling converts the estimate to a summable bound independent of the parameter. Finite-level model potentials extend continuously to the central fibre by Theorem 2.10. Uniform convergence proves continuity and identifies the central escape potential by evaluation of the same iterated homogeneous polynomials. The hybrid model-function extension is requested from TB.0.

### 6.13 Specialising a finitely generated domain to ℚ̄ while keeping finitely many elements nonzero

Let R be a finitely generated ℚ-algebra that is an integral domain and s ∈ R, s ≠ 0. Then there is a ring homomorphism φ : R → ℚ̄ with φ(s) ≠ 0.

R finitely generated over ℚ and a domain; s ≠ 0 (a product of finitely many elements to be kept nonzero, e.g. pairwise differences).

R[1/s] is a nonzero finitely generated ℚ-algebra (Localization.Away), so it has a maximal ideal m (Ideal.exists_maximal). R[1/s]/m is a field finitely generated as a ℚ-algebra, hence finite over ℚ (Zariski's lemma: finite_of_finite_type_of_isJacobsonRing, ℚ being a Jacobson ring). Embed it into ℚ̄ (IsAlgClosed.lift) and compose with R → R[1/s] → R[1/s]/m; s maps to a unit, hence to a nonzero element.

### 6.14 Finite unions of arithmetic progressions in ℕ

A set S ⊆ ℕ is a finite union of arithmetic progressions if there are finitely many pairs (a_i, b_i) ∈ ℕ² with S = ⋃_i {a_i k + b_i : k ∈ ℕ}; the case a_i = 0 contributes the singleton {b_i}, so finite sets qualify. Equivalently, S is eventually periodic: there are N ∈ ℕ and p ≥ 1 with n ∈ S ↔ n + p ∈ S for all n ≥ N.

Arithmetic progressions are one-sided (k ≥ 0) and may have difference 0.

Equivalence: a union of progressions {a_i k + b_i} is periodic with period lcm of the nonzero a_i beyond N = max b_i; conversely an eventually periodic S is the union of the finite set S ∩ [0, N) and the progressions {pk + b} for b ∈ S ∩ [N, N + p). The class is closed under finite unions, intersections and complements (eventually periodic sets form a Boolean algebra).

*Needs:* `mathlib:Set.Finite`; `mathlib:Set.Infinite`.

([bijmst18](#source-parent-bijmst18), §7, before Conjecture 7.1, p. 14 (arXiv v2) — The definition of the node; [bell-ghioca-tucker-2010](#source-parent-bell-ghioca-tucker-2010), Conjecture 1.2, p. 2 (arXiv v1) — The same conjecture in orbit form; equivalent to the arithmetic-progression form (API of DY.6/finite-union-of-arithmetic-progressions).)

The reusable interface consists of the following statements.

- **`IsFiniteUnionAP`** (data): The predicate on sets S ⊆ ℕ.
- **`isFiniteUnionAP_iff_eventually_periodic`** (characterisation): Equivalence with eventual periodicity.
- **`IsFiniteUnionAP.union`** (structure): Closed under binary union.
- **`IsFiniteUnionAP.inter`** (structure): Closed under binary intersection.
- **`IsFiniteUnionAP.compl`** (structure): Closed under complement.
- **`Set.Finite.isFiniteUnionAP`** (constructor): Finite sets are finite unions of arithmetic progressions.
- **`IsFiniteUnionAP.exists_infinite_ap`** (other): An infinite finite union of arithmetic progressions contains {ak + b : k ∈ ℕ} with a ≥ 1.
- **`isFiniteUnionAP_preimage_affine`** (functoriality): If S is one then so is {k : ak + b ∈ S} for a ≥ 1; and S is one iff each {k : Nk + j ∈ S}, 0 ≤ j < N, is one.

**Checks.**

- **`isFiniteUnionAP_evens_union`** (computation): The set {1} ∪ {2k : k ∈ ℕ} is a finite union of arithmetic progressions (pairs (0, 1) and (2, 0)).
- **`isFiniteUnionAP_empty_univ`** (degenerate): The empty set, every finite set and ℕ are finite unions of arithmetic progressions.
- **`isFiniteUnionAP_iff_eventuallyPeriodic`** (compatibility): S is a finite union of arithmetic progressions iff ∃ N, ∃ p ≥ 1, ∀ n ≥ N, (n ∈ S ↔ n + p ∈ S).
- **`not_isFiniteUnionAP_powers`** (non-example): For p ≥ 2, {p^k : k ∈ ℕ} is not a finite union of arithmetic progressions (it is infinite and its gaps are unbounded).

**Endpoint checks.** {0, 1} ∪ 2ℕ is a finite union of arithmetic progressions. {2^k : k ∈ ℕ} is not.

### 6.15 Strassmann's theorem: a nonzero p-adic power series convergent on ℤ_p has finitely many zeros there

Let p be a prime and g(z) = Σ_{i ≥ 0} c_i z^i with c_i ∈ ℚ_p and c_i → 0. If some c_i ≠ 0, let N be the largest index with |c_N|_p = max_i |c_i|_p. Then g has at most N zeros in ℤ_p. In particular a p-adic analytic function on ℤ_p with infinitely many zeros in ℤ_p is identically zero.

Coefficients tend to 0 (convergence on the closed unit disc).

Induction on N. For N = 0: |c_0| > |c_i| for i ≥ 1, so |g(z)| = |c_0| ≠ 0 on ℤ_p by the ultrametric inequality. If g(a) = 0 with a ∈ ℤ_p, write g(z) = g(z) − g(a) = (z − a) h(z) with h(z) = Σ_j (Σ_{i > j} c_i a^{i−1−j}) z^j; the coefficients of h tend to 0, satisfy |h_j| ≤ max_{i > j} |c_i|, and the largest index attaining the maximum of |h_j| is N − 1. By induction h has at most N − 1 zeros, so g has at most N.

*Needs:* `mathlib:PowerSeries`; `mathlib:PadicInt`; `mathlib:IsUltrametricDist`.

### 6.17 p-adic analytic interpolation of orbits (Bell–Ghioca–Tucker Theorem 3.3)

Let p > 3 be prime, n ≥ 1, and ϕ₁, …, ϕ_n ∈ ℤ_p[[x₁, …, x_n]] convergent on ℤ_pⁿ such that (a) ϕ_i ≡ x_i (mod p) and (b) the coefficient of x₁^{k₁}⋯x_n^{k_n} in ϕ_i lies in p^{k₁+⋯+k_n−1} ℤ_p whenever k₁ + ⋯ + k_n ≥ 2. For every ω⃗ ∈ ℤ_pⁿ there are p-adic analytic f₁, …, f_n ∈ ℚ_p[[z]], convergent with |f_i(z)|_p ≤ 1 on |z|_p ≤ 1, with f_i(0) = ω_i and f_i(z + 1) = ϕ_i(f₁(z), …, f_n(z)). In particular (ϕ^k(ω⃗))_i = f_i(k) for k ∈ ℕ.

p > 3; hypotheses (a), (b).

Work in the ring C of Mahler series Σ c_i binom(z, i) with c_i → 0 (the continuous functions ℤ_p → ℤ_p, Mahler) and its subring B of Mahler polynomials. Construct h_{i,j} ∈ B inductively with h_{i,0} = ω_i, h_{i,j}(0) = 0 and deg h_{i,j} ≤ 2j − 1 for j ≥ 1, such that g_{i,j} = Σ_{k ≤ j} p^k h_{i,k} satisfies g_{i,j}(z + 1) ≡ ϕ_i(g_{·,j}(z)) mod p^{j+1}C (BGT Lemma 3.2 controls the products of the correction terms). The limits f_i = lim_j g_{i,j} converge and satisfy the functional equation; the degree bound 2j − 1 against p^j and p > 3 give analyticity on |z|_p ≤ 1.

### 6.18 Prime divisors of polynomial values avoiding prescribed primes

For a nonconstant f ∈ ℤ[X], a nonzero integer m and N ∈ ℕ, there are a prime p > N and a ∈ ℤ such that p ∤ m and p ∣ f(a). Equivalently, the reduction of f has a root for arbitrarily large primes outside any prescribed finite set.

The polynomial has positive natural degree; m ≠ 0. No separability or irreducibility is assumed.

Put c = f(0) and M = N!·m ≠ 0. If c = 0, take a = 0 and use Nat.exists_infinite_primes above max(N, |m|); such a prime cannot divide m. When c ≠ 0, let a vary through the infinite set cMℤ. Polynomial.tendstoCofinite_of_natDegree_ne_zero implies that only finitely many such a have f(a) in the finite integer interval [−|c|, |c|]. Choose a = cMt outside that preimage. Polynomial.sub_dvd_eval_sub at a and 0 gives f(a) − c = cMt·k for an integer k. Hence f(a) = c·r with r = 1 + Mt·k and |r| > 1. Nat.ne_one_iff_exists_prime_dvd applied to |r| gives a prime p dividing r. A divisor of M cannot divide r ≡ 1 modulo M, so p ∤ M. In particular p ∤ m; if p ≤ N then p divides N!, a contradiction. Finally p ∣ f(a). This is the addendum's elementary proof, with the finite exclusions encoded in M.

*Needs:* `mathlib:Polynomial.tendstoCofinite_of_natDegree_ne_zero`; `mathlib:Polynomial.sub_dvd_eval_sub`; `mathlib:Nat.ne_one_iff_exists_prime_dvd`; `mathlib:Nat.exists_infinite_primes`.

**Endpoint checks.** f = X has a = 0 for every prime; the zero constant term must not trigger division by zero. f = X² + 1, m = 6, N = 3 admits p = 5, a = 2. The lemma does not assert that every p > N works. A constant polynomial 1 has no prime divisor at any value and is excluded by the degree hypothesis.

Evaluating the identity gives A(Y,a)H(Y,a) + B(Y,a)∂YH(Y,a) = c(a).

If P vanished on every a ∈ ℤⁿ, MvPolynomial.funext over the infinite domain ℤ would imply P = 0. Choose a with P(a) ≠ 0 and extract all factor nonvanishings. This works also for n = 0 and empty D. ### 6.20 Hensel lifting from a simple residue-field root

Let p be prime, F ∈ ℤ_p[X] and b ∈ ℤ_p. If the reductions of F(b) and F′(b) in 𝔽_p are respectively zero and nonzero, then there is z ∈ ℤ_p with F(z) = 0, z mod p = b mod p and F′(z) a unit in ℤ_p.

The reduction map is Mathlib's PadicInt.toZMod. This holds also for p = 2; the later analytic interpolation restriction p ≥ 5 is separate.

PadicInt.ker_toZMod identifies zero reduction with membership in the maximal ideal; PadicInt.mem_nonunits identifies this with norm strictly less than one. PadicInt.norm_le_one then turns nonzero derivative reduction into derivative norm exactly one. Apply hensels_lemma to the strict inequality ‖F(b)‖ < ‖F′(b)‖². Use its root and closeness conclusions, and equality of derivative norms at z and b. Closeness ‖z − b‖ < 1 gives equality of reductions through the kernel description. PadicInt.isUnit_iff converts derivative norm one to the final unit assertion.

### 6.25 Call–Silverman specialization over a global height field and a curve

Let K be a global height field with its chosen product-formula height structure, T/K a smooth projective geometrically integral curve, and h_T a nonnegative Weil height for a divisor of degree 1. Let V/K be smooth and projective and π:V→T a morphism with smooth geometrically integral generic fibre, P a rational section, and φ a rational self-map over T that is a morphism on the generic fibre. Let η∈Pic(V)⊗R and α>1, with φ*η−αη represented by a fibral divisor (supported over a proper closed subset of T), using the rational pullback convention of Call–Silverman §3. On a nonempty good open U where the fibres are smooth and geometrically integral and φ_t is a morphism, one has lim_{h_T(t)→∞, t∈U(K̄)} ĥ_{V_t,η_t,φ_t}(P_t)/h_T(t)=ĥ_{V_η,η_η,φ_η}(P_η). The right side uses the degree-normalized geometric height on K(T). The statement does not assert an O(1) error.

Use compatible height normalizations under finite extensions. The section is evaluated where defined. A projective model lets rational sections extend over the smooth curve. A specified global height field is required; finite generation of K alone does not specify a height. Ampleness of η is not needed for the eigenclass limit.

The relative canonical/Weil-height difference is ≤C₁h_T(t)+C₂ by the general-curve version of Theorem 3.1; its constants are uniform in the point on the fibre. For each fixed section Q=φⁿP, functoriality gives h_{V,η}(Q_t)=h_{T,Q*η}(t)+O_Q(1). Generic intersection degree equals the geometric Weil height of Q_η. Use curve-height quasi-equivalence h_{T,D}(t)/h_T(t)→deg D, including real divisor classes; the height and intersection contracts are requested from RP.0. Combining with the generic canonical/Weil bound gives a limsup error bounded independently of Q after section-dependent O(1) terms vanish. Replace P by φⁿP. Both canonical heights multiply by αⁿ. Divide the uniform limsup bound by αⁿ and let n tend to infinity. This generalizes the inherited t-line endpoint without requiring Northcott over K.

### 6.26 Equal-degree Bilu–Tichy classification input

If K is a number field, S a finite set of nonarchimedean places, F,G∈K[X] have equal degree >1 and F(x)=G(y) has infinitely many S-integral solutions, then F=E∘F₁∘a and G=E∘G₁∘b for E∈K[X] and affine a,b∈K[X], where, up to interchanging F₁,G₁, the pair is (X,X), (X²,c∘X²) with affine c, (D₂(X,α)/α,D₂(X,β)/β) with nonzero α,β∈K, or (D_n(X,α),−D_n(X cos(π/n),α)) with α∈K and cos(2π/n)∈K. D_n is the Dickson polynomial characterized by D_n(U+V,UV)=Uⁿ+Vⁿ.

n is a positive integer, parameters are interpreted in a chosen algebraic closure in the fourth case. Only the equal-degree necessity is needed.

Siegel bounds the genus and number of points at infinity of a component with infinitely many S-integral points. Bilu–Tichy classify the resulting genus-zero polynomial pairs through polynomial decomposition. This classification proof is not given in GTZ and is retained as a precise gap. For the downstream shape corollary, normalize nonzero Dickson parameters by a square root over K̄. Up to affine composition, a common H is Xⁿ or D_n(X,1); the cyclotomic degree bound makes the admissible n finite for fixed K.

### 6.27 The dynamical Lehmer conjecture for maps of ℙ¹ (statement)

For a number field K and a rational map f of ℙ¹ of degree d ≥ 2 over K, the dynamical Lehmer property Lehmer(f) says: there is C(f) > 0 such that ĥ_f(x) ≥ C(f)/[K(x) : K] for every x ∈ ℙ¹(ℚ̄) that is not preperiodic for f, where ĥ_f is the absolute canonical height (DY.1/canonical-height-on-the-projective-line). The dynamical Lehmer conjecture (for ℙ¹) is the proposition that Lehmer(f) holds for every such K and f. It is a statement, not a theorem; no node of this roadmap assumes it except as an explicit hypothesis.

K a number field; d ≥ 2; x ranges over ℚ̄-points that are wandering. The ℙ^N form of the source is the same statement for morphisms of ℙ^N; DY.6 states the ℙ¹ case, which is the case its examples use.

The degree [K(x) : K] of the field of definition of x; wandering means not preperiodic. For f = z² the property is Lehmer's conjecture ∃ C > 0, h(α) ≥ C/[ℚ(α) : ℚ] for α ≠ 0 not a root of unity (ClassicalArithmeticCompletion:CA.6/canonical-height-power-map).

### 6.28 Dynamically related points of a map over a function field

Let L be a field with algebraic closure L̄, f a rational map of ℙ¹ of degree d ≥ 2 over L with forms (F, G), and a, b ∈ ℙ¹(L̄). The points a and b are f-dynamically related if there is a nonzero squarefree bihomogeneous Q ∈ L̄[X₀, X₁; Y₀, Y₁] of positive total degree (defining a curve C = V(Q) ⊂ ℙ¹ × ℙ¹) with Q(a; b) = 0 and (f × f)(C) ⊆ C, i.e. Q divides Q(F(X₀, X₁), G(X₀, X₁); F(Y₀, Y₁), G(Y₀, Y₁)). For a family over k(t) (DY.6/specialization-of-rational-maps) one takes L = k(t).

L any field; in the dynamical André–Oort conjecture L = k(t) with k algebraically closed of characteristic 0.

For squarefree Q, the invariance (f × f)(C) ⊆ C is equivalent to Q | Q ∘ (F, G; F, G) by the Nullstellensatz over L̄.

### 6.29 Integral primitive presentation with marked elements

For every field L of characteristic zero, finitely generated over Q, and finite marked family s:I→L, there exist n≥0, a transcendence basis t:Fin n→L, a primitive element y, an injective evaluation j: A=Z[T₁,…,Tₙ]→L, its extension ĵ:F=Frac(A)→L, and H∈A[Y], with L=ĵ(F)(y), H(y,t)=0, deg_Y H>0, and H_F a nonzero scalar multiple of the monic minimal polynomial of y over F. Thus H_F is irreducible and separable. There are U_i∈A[Y] and V_i∈A\{0} with s_i=U_i(y,t)/V_i(t). One may choose deg_Y U_i<deg_Y H and a single common V for all i. A marked zero has numerator zero; the marked family is independent of any generating family.

Algebra.EssFiniteType Q L; I finite, possibly empty. Neither a presentation nor an embedding is assumed. A has integer coefficients; the denominators V have no primitive-element variable. The equation H need not be monic.

Choose the finite transcendence basis and identify Q(t) with Frac(Q[T]) by aevalEquivField. Frac(Z[T]) and Frac(Q[T]) identify by their fraction-field universal properties: each rational coefficient is an integer divided by a nonzero integer. This identifies ĵ(F) with Q(t). L is algebraic over Q(t) by the transcendence-basis property. A finite field-generating set for L over Q also generates over Q(t), so this algebraic extension is finite (finite_of_essFiniteType_of_isAlgebraic). Characteristic zero gives separability; choose y by the primitive-element theorem. Use its power basis to write each s_i as a polynomial of degree below [L:F] in y. Clear the finite set of coefficients in F simultaneously by exist_integer_multiples. The denominator is in A, not in A[Y]. Integer-normalize the monic minimal polynomial to H. Its image is c times that polynomial with c≠0. Multiplication by c does not change degree, roots, irreducibility or separability over F. Transport the power-basis equalities through ĵ to obtain the marked identities.

### 6.30 Disc covering at a place of bad polynomial reduction

Over a complete algebraically closed nonarchimedean field, a polynomial f of degree d≥2 and leading coefficient a_d has filled Julia set contained in a unique smallest closed disc of radius r≥ρ=|a_d|^{-1/(d−1)}. Potential good reduction is equivalent to r=ρ. If r>ρ and z₀ is in the filled Julia set, that set is contained in the union of open discs D(x,ρ) for x∈f^{-2}(z₀), at most d² discs.

The absolute value is nonarchimedean and the field is complete and algebraically closed. At potentially good places the containing disc is closed; at bad places the final covering discs are open.

The smallest-disc and inverse-disc theorems are the precise local input of Benedetto Lemmas 5.1–5.2. Their proofs are referenced there to the earlier local filled-Julia paper and remain a recorded gap. For the covering conclusion, two inverse-image discs at distance r force in each fibre at least one second preimage at distance ≥r from a point outside all open radius-ρ discs. Factor f(z)−y and then f²(z)−z₀. The product bounds imply |f²(z)−z₀|>r for such a point, excluding it from the filled Julia set (Lemma 5.3).

*Needs:* [`ArithmeticDynamics:DY.2/escape-rate`](#target-arithmeticdynamics-dy-2-escape-rate).

### 6.31 Preperiodic and periodic points of the power map

Let K be a field and d ≥ 2. A point x ∈ ℙ¹(K) is preperiodic for P_d if and only if x ∈ {0, ∞} or x is a root of unity. It is periodic if and only if x ∈ {0, ∞} or x is a root of unity whose order is prime to d; a root of unity of order N prime to d has exact period the multiplicative order of d modulo N.

K any field; d ≥ 2.

0 and ∞ are fixed. If x ≠ 0, ∞ and P_d^m(x) = P_d^n(x) with m < n, then x^{d^m} = x^{d^n}, so x^{d^m(d^{n−m} − 1)} = 1 with a positive exponent; x has finite order (isOfFinOrder_iff_pow_eq_one). Conversely if x has finite order N, all iterates x^{dⁿ} lie in the finite group generated by x, so two coincide and x is preperiodic. x (of order N) is periodic iff x^{dⁿ} = x for some n ≥ 1 iff N | dⁿ − 1 for some n ≥ 1 (orderOf_dvd_iff_pow_eq_one); this forces gcd(N, d) = 1, and conversely gcd(N, d) = 1 gives d^{φ(N)} ≡ 1 (mod N) (Nat.ModEq.pow_totient). The least such n is the order of d in (ℤ/N)^×.

### 6.32 Escape rate, local canonical heights and canonical measure of the power map

Let d ≥ 2, let K be a number field and v a place of K, and let F_d(z, w) = (z^d, w^d) be the homogeneous lift of P_d. Then the escape rate (DY.2/escape-rate) is G_{F_d,v}(z, w) = log max{|z|_v, |w|_v} for all (z, w) ∈ ℂ_v², the local canonical height (DY.2/local-canonical-height) is λ_{P_d,v}(x) = log⁺|x|_v, and the canonical measure (DY.2/canonical-measure) is μ_{P_d,v} = ω_v: the normalised Haar measure on the unit circle when v is archimedean and the point mass at the Gauss point ζ_{0,1} when v is nonarchimedean.

d ≥ 2; K a number field with a place v; ℂ_v the completion of an algebraic closure of K_v. The Laplacian is normalised by Δ log⁺|z|_v = ω_v − δ_∞ (DY.2/canonical-measure).

F_dⁿ(z, w) = (z^{dⁿ}, w^{dⁿ}) and max{|z|^{dⁿ}, |w|^{dⁿ}} = max{|z|, |w|}^{dⁿ}, so d^{−n} log ‖F_dⁿ(z, w)‖_v = log ‖(z, w)‖_v for every n and the limit is attained at n = 0. λ_{P_d,v}(x) = G_{F_d,v}(x, 1) = log max{|x|_v, 1} = log⁺|x|_v. The canonical measure is Δλ + δ_∞ = Δ log⁺|z|_v + δ_∞ = ω_v by the normalisation of the Laplacian (DY.2/canonical-measure).

<a id="target-arithmeticdynamics-dy-6-power-map-dynatomic-polynomials"></a>

### 6.33 Dynatomic polynomials of the power map are products of cyclotomic polynomials

Let K be a field of characteristic 0 and d ≥ 2. For n ≥ 1, the affine part of the n-th dynatomic polynomial (DY.3/dynatomic-polynomial) of P_d is Φ*_n(P_d)(z) = z^{[n = 1]} · ∏_{m} Φ_m(z), the product over all m ≥ 1 with gcd(m, d) = 1 and ord_m(d) = n, where Φ_m is the m-th cyclotomic polynomial and ord_m(d) the order of d in (ℤ/m)^×; the point ∞ is a root only for n = 1. Every root has multiplicity one, and the points of formal period n (DY.3/formal-and-exact-period) are exactly the points of exact period n.

char K = 0 (so that the cyclotomic polynomials are separable and d is a unit). d ≥ 2, n ≥ 1.

For k ≥ 1, z^{d^k} − z = z (z^{d^k − 1} − 1) = z ∏_{m | d^k − 1} Φ_m(z) (Polynomial.prod_cyclotomic_eq_X_pow_sub_one). In the Möbius product Φ*_n = ∏_{k | n} (z^{d^k} − z)^{μ(n/k)} the exponent of z is Σ_{k|n} μ(n/k) = [n = 1], and the exponent of Φ_m is Σ_{k | n, r | k} μ(n/k) with r = ord_m(d) (since m | d^k − 1 iff r | k); this sum is [n = r] (Möbius inversion, ArithmeticFunction.moebius). The cyclotomic factors are pairwise coprime and separable in characteristic 0, so all roots are simple; a simple root of Φ*_n has exact period n (DY.3/formal-and-exact-period).

<a id="target-arithmeticdynamics-dy-6-power-map-preimage-tree"></a>

### 6.34 The preimage tree of the power map and its Kummer Galois action

Let K be a field of characteristic 0, d ≥ 2 and a ∈ K^×. The n-th level of the preimage tree (DY.5/preimage-tree) of P_d at a is P_d^{−n}(a) = {β : β^{dⁿ} = a}, of size dⁿ. Choose a compatible system (β_n) with β_{n+1}^d = β_n, β_0 = a, and a compatible system (ζ_{dⁿ}) of primitive dⁿ-th roots of unity with ζ_{d^{n+1}}^d = ζ_{dⁿ}; then level n is {ζ_{dⁿ}^i β_n : i ∈ ℤ/dⁿ}, and every σ ∈ Gal(K̄/K) acts by ζ_{dⁿ}^i β_n ↦ ζ_{dⁿ}^{χ(σ) i + b_n(σ)} β_n, where χ is the cyclotomic character mod dⁿ and σ(β_n) = ζ_{dⁿ}^{b_n(σ)} β_n. Hence the arboreal representation (DY.5/arboreal-galois-representation) of (P_d, a) takes values in the affine group {i ↦ u i + b : u ∈ ℤ_d^×, b ∈ ℤ_d} of the tree lim ℤ/dⁿ, a subgroup of infinite index in the tree automorphism group for d ≥ 2.

char K = 0 (so that x^{dⁿ} − a is separable for a ≠ 0). a ≠ 0 (at a = 0 the tree collapses).

x^{dⁿ} − a is separable (its derivative dⁿx^{dⁿ−1} vanishes only at 0, not a root), so level n has dⁿ points, and they are ζ^i β_n for the dⁿ-th roots of unity ζ^i. σ(ζ_{dⁿ}) = ζ_{dⁿ}^{χ(σ)} and σ(β_n) is again a root of x^{dⁿ} − a, so σ(β_n) = ζ_{dⁿ}^{b_n(σ)} β_n; multiplicativity gives the displayed formula. Compatibility of the β_n and ζ_{dⁿ} under x ↦ x^d makes (χ(σ), b_n(σ)) compatible in n, giving the affine group over ℤ_d = lim ℤ/dⁿ. At level n the affine group has order dⁿφ(dⁿ), at most d²ⁿ. The full rooted tree group has order (d!)^{(dⁿ−1)/(d−1)} (DY.5/tree-automorphism-order), so the indices of the images tend to infinity. Do not assert strict containment at every n≥2: for d=2,n=2 both groups have order 8. Use the preceding order comparison at arbitrarily large levels to conclude infinite index. Binary depth two is an equality case, so a claim of strict containment at every depth n ≥ 2 would be false.

The arboreal representation of z² at 2 is not surjective onto the tree automorphisms: a finite computation at level 3 certifies it.

### 6.35 The Lattès map semiconjugates multiplication by n

Let F be a field, E/F a Weierstrass curve with Δ(E) ≠ 0, n ≠ 0, and x : E(F) → ℙ¹(F) the x-coordinate (Mathlib WeierstrassCurve.Affine.Point.xRep: x(O) = [1 : 0] = ∞, x(x₀, y₀) = [x₀ : 1]). Then f_{E,n}(x(P)) = x(nP) for every P ∈ E(F). Equivalently, for an affine point P = (x₀, y₀): ΨSq_n(x₀) = 0 if and only if nP = O, and otherwise x(nP) = Φ_n(x₀)/ΨSq_n(x₀).

Δ(E) ≠ 0 and n ≠ 0.

P = O: f_{E,n}(∞) = ∞ = x(O) (DY.6/lattes-map). P = (x₀, y₀) and nP = (x₁, y₁) affine: x₁ · ΨSq_n(x₀) = Φ_n(x₀) (WeierstrassCurve.mul_eval_ΨSq_eq_eval_Φ_of_zsmul) and ΨSq_n(x₀) ≠ 0 (WeierstrassCurve.eval_ΨSq_ne_zero_of_zsmul_ne_zero), so f_{E,n}(x₀) = Φ_n(x₀)/ΨSq_n(x₀) = x₁. P = (x₀, y₀) affine with nP = O: ψ_n(x₀, y₀) = 0 (WeierstrassCurve.evalEval_ψ_eq_zero_of_zsmul_eq_zero, transporting nP = O to the Jacobian model), hence ΨSq_n(x₀) = ψ_n(x₀, y₀)² = 0 (WeierstrassCurve.evalEval_ψ_eq_evalEval_Ψ, WeierstrassCurve.evalEval_Ψ_sq_eq_eval_ΨSq); by coprimality Φ_n(x₀) ≠ 0 (WeierstrassCurve.isCoprime_Φ_ΨSq), so f_{E,n}(x₀) = [Φ_n(x₀) : 0] = ∞ = x(O).

### 6.36 The Legendre curve E_t and its Lattès map f_t

Let F be a field of characteristic ≠ 2 and t ∈ F with t ≠ 0, 1. The Legendre curve E_t : y² = x(x − 1)(x − t) is the Mathlib Weierstrass curve with a₁ = a₃ = a₆ = 0, a₂ = −(1 + t), a₄ = t; its discriminant is Δ(E_t) = 16t²(t − 1)² and its j-invariant is j(t) = 256(t² − t + 1)³/(t²(t − 1)²). The Legendre Lattès map is f_t := f_{E_t,2} (DY.6/lattes-map): f_t(x) = (x² − t)²/(4x(x − 1)(x − t)), a rational map of degree 4 with homogeneous lift F_t(z, w) = ((z² − tw²)², 4zw(z − w)(z − tw)). For F = ℚ̄, the Legendre canonical height is ĥ_t := ĥ_{f_t} (DY.1/canonical-height-on-the-projective-line).

char F ≠ 2 (for char 2 the curve y² = x(x − 1)(x − t) is singular). t ≠ 0, 1 (exactly the condition Δ(E_t) ≠ 0 when char F ≠ 2).

b₂ = −4(1 + t), b₄ = 2t, b₆ = 0, b₈ = −t², so Φ_2 = x⁴ − 2tx² + t² = (x² − t)² and ΨSq_2 = 4x³ − 4(1 + t)x² + 4tx = 4x(x − 1)(x − t) (WeierstrassCurve.Φ_two, WeierstrassCurve.ΨSq_two). Δ(E_t) = 16t²(t − 1)² and j(t) = 256(t² − t + 1)³/(t²(t − 1)²) from Mathlib's formulas WeierstrassCurve.Δ and WeierstrassCurve.j. Homogenising Φ_2 and ΨSq_2 in degree 4 gives F_t.

### 6.37 The height bound for a rational map over k(t)

Let k be a field and f a rational map of ℙ¹ of degree d ≥ 1 over k(t), given by coprime forms F, G ∈ k(t)[X, Y] of degree d. There is C_f ≥ 0 such that |h_{k(t)}(f(P)) − d · h_{k(t)}(P)| ≤ C_f for all P ∈ ℙ¹(k(t)).

k any field; the height is the degree height of DY.6/rational-function-field-heights.

Upper bound: Mathlib Height.logHeight_eval_le for the family (F, G) with the instance of DY.6/rational-function-field-heights: h(f(P)) ≤ d h(P) + log max(mulHeightBound (F, G), 1). Lower bound: the resultant certificate A₁F + B₁G = Res·X^{2d−1}, A₂F + B₂G = Res·Y^{2d−1} (DY.0/resultant-of-a-rational-map; Mathlib Polynomial.exists_mul_add_mul_eq_C_resultant after dehomogenising), divided by Res ∈ k(t)^×, is a family q as in Mathlib Height.logHeight_eval_ge; since totalWeight = 0 the constant is log max(mulHeightBound q, 1). Take C_f the larger of the two constants.

### 6.38 Specialisation commutes with evaluation and iteration

In the setting of DY.6/specialization-of-rational-maps, for every t₀ ∈ T⁰(f) and P ∈ ℙ¹(k(t)): (f(P))_{t₀} = f_{t₀}(P_{t₀}), and hence (fⁿ(P))_{t₀} = f_{t₀}ⁿ(P_{t₀}) for all n ≥ 0.

t₀ ∈ T⁰(f), i.e. Res(F, G)(t₀) ≠ 0.

Write P = [p : q] with p, q ∈ k[t] coprime; then f(P) = [F(p, q) : G(p, q)], and a primitive representative is obtained by dividing by g = gcd(F(p, q), G(p, q)) ∈ k[t]. Evaluating the resultant certificate A₁F + B₁G = Res·X^{2d−1}, A₂F + B₂G = Res·Y^{2d−1} (with A_i, B_i ∈ k[t][X, Y]) at (p, q) shows g | Res·p^{2d−1} and g | Res·q^{2d−1}; as gcd(p, q) = 1, g | Res(F, G) (DY.0/resultant-of-a-rational-map, Mathlib Polynomial.exists_mul_add_mul_eq_C_resultant). For t₀ ∈ T⁰(f), g(t₀) ≠ 0, so (f(P))_{t₀} = [F(p, q)(t₀) : G(p, q)(t₀)] = [F_{t₀}(p(t₀), q(t₀)) : G_{t₀}(p(t₀), q(t₀))] = f_{t₀}(P_{t₀}). Induction on n, using that fⁿ(P) ∈ ℙ¹(k(t)).

### 6.39 Height bounds for forms in absolute normalisation, uniform in the field

Let K be a number field, N, M ≥ 0, and p = (p_j)_{j ∈ J} a finite family of homogeneous polynomials of degree N in variables indexed by a finite type ι, with coefficients in K. For a number field L ⊇ K and x ∈ L^ι ∖ {0}, write h(x) := Height.logHeight_L(x)/[L : ℚ] (independent of L by DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.0/mul-height-algebra-map). ### 6.44 The dynamical Mordell–Lang conjecture (statement)

For a quasi-projective variety X over ℂ, a morphism Φ : X → X, a closed subvariety V ⊆ X and a point α ∈ X(ℂ), let S(X, Φ, V, α) = {n ∈ ℕ : Φⁿ(α) ∈ V(ℂ)}. The dynamical Mordell–Lang property DML(X, Φ) says that S(X, Φ, V, α) is a finite union of arithmetic progressions (DY.6/finite-union-of-arithmetic-progressions) for every V and α. The dynamical Mordell–Lang conjecture is the proposition that DML(X, Φ) holds for every quasi-projective X over ℂ and every endomorphism Φ. It is a statement, not a theorem: no node of this roadmap assumes it except as an explicit hypothesis. The affine special case DML_affine(N): for every polynomial map Φ : 𝔸^N_ℂ → 𝔸^N_ℂ, every finite family G of polynomials and every α ∈ ℂ^N, {n : g(Φⁿ(α)) = 0 for all g ∈ G} is a finite union of arithmetic progressions.

Characteristic 0 is essential: DY.6/dml-fails-in-positive-characteristic. Quasi-projective varieties and their morphisms are those of SchemeAndStackFoundations:SF.0 (the requests list the precise need).

The two formulations agree: V(ℂ) ∩ O_Φ(α) is a finite union of orbits O_{Φ^N}(Φ^ℓ(α)) iff S is a finite union of progressions {Nk + ℓ} (DY.6/finite-union-of-arithmetic-progressions). DML_affine(N) is the case X = 𝔸^N_ℂ, V = V(G).

### 6.45 The dynamical Mordell–Lang statement fails in positive characteristic (Ghioca Example 1.4)

Let p be prime, K = 𝔽_p(t), V ⊂ 𝔾_m² the curve tx + (1 − t)y = 1, Φ(x, y) = (t^{p²−1}x, (1 − t)^{p²−1}y) and α = (1, 1). Then {n ∈ ℕ : Φⁿ(α) ∈ V} = {(p^{2j} − 1)/(p² − 1) : j ∈ ℕ}, which is infinite but not a finite union of arithmetic progressions.

K = 𝔽_p(t); Φ is an automorphism (a translation) of 𝔾_m², hence étale.

Φⁿ(α) = (t^{n(p²−1)}, (1 − t)^{n(p²−1)}) lies on V iff t^m + (1 − t)^m = 1 with m = n(p² − 1) + 1. If m = p^k then t^m + (1 − t)^m = (t + 1 − t)^{p^k} = 1 (Frobenius, add_pow_char_pow). Conversely write m = p^k m′ with p ∤ m′; if m′ > 1, then with u = t^{p^k} the polynomial u^{m′} + (1 − u)^{m′} − 1 has coefficient −m′ ≠ 0 at u¹, so it is nonzero and t^m + (1 − t)^m ≠ 1. m = p^k ≡ 1 (mod p² − 1) iff k is even (p ≢ 1 mod p² − 1), giving n = (p^{2j} − 1)/(p² − 1). The gaps between consecutive elements are unbounded, so the set contains no infinite arithmetic progression with positive difference and is not a finite union of arithmetic progressions (DY.6/finite-union-of-arithmetic-progressions).

### 6.46 Common iterates from synchronized affine intersections

Let K have characteristic zero, f(X)=aX+b and g(X)=cX+e with a,c nonzero. If the set of common values fⁿ(x₀)=gⁿ(y₀), with the same n≥0, is infinite, then f^{∘m}=g^{∘m} for some m≥1. Together with conjugating a nonvertical line to the diagonal, this supplies the linear case of the inherited polynomial-lines DML target.

Infinitude concerns distinct common values, not merely infinitely many time indices. Both slopes are nonzero; constant maps have finite synchronized image.

Reduce to the finitely generated characteristic-zero subfield containing the coefficients and initial points, embed it in C, and shift to a first common value. A nontrivial root-of-unity slope has a finite orbit and is excluded by distinct-value infinitude. If both slopes differ from 1, write the two iterates using their fixed-point translations. If the translated starting values differ, their equality becomes A aⁿ+B cⁿ=1 with A,B nonzero. The finitely generated multiplicative subgroup generated by a,c meets the exact DT.2 two-variable unit-equation contract; distinct n give distinct solutions because a is not a root of unity. Thus the translated starting values coincide, forcing equal fixed points and aⁿ=cⁿ at a return, hence equality of the corresponding affine iterates. If both slopes are 1, equality after shifting to a common start forces the two translation increments to coincide. If exactly one slope is 1, the nontrivial translation grows linearly along the common-return subsequence. A slope of complex modulus at most 1 gives a bounded other orbit; one of modulus greater than 1 grows exponentially. Either contradicts infinitely many returns (GTZ Proposition 5.3). GTZ Lemma 5.1 handles nonvertical lines by affine conjugation; a vertical or horizontal line with infinitely many distinct orbit points is periodic because the relevant coordinate is periodic. Use the inherited finite-union-of-progressions contract for time sets.

### 6.48 Simple roots modulo primes from an integral Bézout certificate

Let f,A,B ∈ ℤ[X], deg f > 0, and c,m ∈ ℤ be nonzero. If Af + Bf′ = c as polynomials, then for every N there are a prime p > N, with p ∤ m, and a ∈ ℤ such that f(a) ≡ 0 modulo p but f′(a) is nonzero modulo p.

In the Cassels consumer, DY.6/lech-integral-specialization-certificate now constructs the integral certificate and an admissible specialization from the generically separable integral equation. ### 6.49 Hensel specialization preserving degree and denominator units

Let p be prime, n ≥ 0, H ∈ ℤ[T₁,…,Tₙ][Y], a ∈ ℤⁿ, ξ ∈ ℤ_pⁿ with ξ mod p = a mod p, and b ∈ ℤ. Put H_a = H(Y,a) and F = H(Y,ξ) ∈ ℤ_p[Y]. Assume p divides H_a(b), p does not divide H_a′(b), and p does not divide lc(H)(a). Let D be a finite set of parameter polynomials with p not dividing q(a) for all q ∈ D. There is η ∈ ℤ_p with F(η) = 0, η mod p = b mod p, F′(η) a unit, deg F = deg H, lc(H)(ξ) a unit, and q(ξ) a unit for all q ∈ D.

Neither generic separability nor independence of ξ is needed for this statement: the displayed simple residue root is sufficient. H need not be monic. D may be empty. All degrees are natural degrees, with the leading coefficient condition excluding zero H.

Compare the two ring homomorphisms ℤ[T] → 𝔽_p: reduction after evaluation at ξ, and integer evaluation at a followed by reduction. MvPolynomial.comp_eval₂Hom, together with the coordinate congruences and preservation of integer constants, makes them equal. Thus every Q satisfies red(Q(ξ)) = Q(a) mod p. This is direct use of the existing polynomial universal property, not an extra generic polynomial-evaluation node. Polynomial.map_map and eval_map_apply transport this equality to H and evaluation at b. Polynomial.derivative_map supplies the same identity for H′. ZMod.intCast_zmod_eq_zero_iff_dvd converts the two divisibility assumptions into F(b) reducing to zero and F′(b) reducing to a nonzero element. Apply DY.6/hensel-root-of-simple-reduction. It returns an integral root η in the residue class b and a unit F′(η). No step infers a simple root merely from existence of a residue root. ### 6.50 Independent p-adic parameters in prescribed residue classes

For a prime p, n ≥ 0 and any a : Fin n → ℤ there is ξ : Fin n → ℤ_p such that its image in ℚ_p is algebraically independent over ℚ and ξ_i mod p = a_i mod p for every i. Reduction is PadicInt.toZMod. In particular an integral tuple of residue representatives need not itself be independent.

No restriction on p beyond primality. Independence is stated after coercion ℤ_p → ℚ_p; ℤ_p is not treated as a ℚ-algebra. The empty tuple is permitted.

Take θ in ℚ_p from DY.6/lech-padic-independent-family. Since ‖p‖ < 1, tendsto_pow_atTop_nhds_zero_of_norm_lt_one and continuity of multiplication imply p^t θ_i → 0 as t → ∞. For each i choose t_i ∈ ℕ with ‖p^{t_i}θ_i‖ < 1. This choice may vary with i. Apply DY.6/lech-affine-independent-family with rational translations a_i and nonzero rational scalars p^{t_i}. It gives independence of ξ_i = a_i + p^{t_i}θ_i inside ℚ_p; prime p is nonzero in ℚ. Each integer a_i has norm at most one, as the coercion of its native ℤ_p value. Padic.nonarchimedean makes ‖ξ_i‖ ≤ 1, so ξ_i defines an actual element of PadicInt. No surrogate p-adic carrier is introduced. The difference ξ_i − a_i has norm strictly less than one. PadicInt.mem_nonunits and the local-ring maximal-ideal characterization put it in the kernel PadicInt.ker_toZMod, yielding the required reduction equality. Coercing back to ℚ_p preserves the family just constructed.

### 6.51 The dynamical André–Oort conjecture for one-parameter families (statement)

Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0 and f a rational map of degree d ≥ 2 over k(t) (a family over the t-line, DY.6/specialization-of-rational-maps) that is not isotrivial in moduli: the specialisations f_{t₀}, t₀ ∈ T⁰(f), are not all conjugate to one another. Let c₁, …, c_{2d−2} ∈ ℙ¹ over an algebraic closure of k(t) be the critical points of f with multiplicity (DY.0/critical-points-of-a-rational-map). DAO(f) is the equivalence: there are infinitely many t₀ ∈ T⁰(f) such that f_{t₀} is postcritically finite (DY.6/postcritically-finite-map) if and only if c_i and c_j are f-dynamically related (DY.6/dynamically-related-points) for all i, j. The dynamical André–Oort conjecture for one-parameter families (Baker–DeMarco) is the proposition that DAO(f) holds for all such families. It is a statement, not a theorem; the higher-dimensional form of Baker–DeMarco is not precise in the sources and is not stated in DY.6.

Base: the t-line, with f defined over k(t); passing to a finite cover of the base on which the critical points are rational does not change either side, so this is the source's statement for families defined over k(t). k algebraically closed of characteristic 0. The non-isotriviality hypothesis is implicit in the source (its families (11.1) are non-constant); without it the statement is false (ArithmeticDynamics/E710).

(b) ⟹ (a) is expected from relations forcing simultaneous preperiodicity; (a) ⟹ (b) is the unlikely-intersection content. Neither direction is proved in general. Both sides are unchanged by a finite base change t = φ(s) and by conjugation of the family, so the formulation with critical points over the algebraic closure of k(t) agrees with the marked-critical-point formulation of the source.

### 6.52 Transport through a primitive root

Let A be a domain with F=Frac(A), let L/F be a finite simple extension generated by y, and let j:A→L be its scalar map. Suppose H∈A[Y] maps to C(c)·minpoly_F(y), c≠0. For any field E, injective e:A→E, and η∈E with H_e(η)=0, there is a unique ring homomorphism σ:L→E extending e on A and sending y to η. It is injective. Every marked identity x=U_j(y)/j(V) with V≠0 transports to σ(x)=U_e(η)/e(V).

The F-algebra structure on L is compatible with A; y is integral over F and F(y)=L. E need not be algebraically closed. Irreducibility is over the embedded parameter field ê(F), not over E.

Extend e uniquely to ê:F→E by IsFractionRing.lift; the map is injective. Give E the F-algebra structure through ê. Map H_F=C(c) minpoly to E. Since ê(c)≠0, the root equation implies minpoly_F(y) evaluated at η is zero. Use algHomAdjoinIntegralEquiv (equivalently adjoinRootEquivAdjoin followed by root evaluation), then identify F(y) with L. The generator-value lemma gives σ(y)=η. A field homomorphism is injective. Any other extension agrees on F by fraction-field uniqueness and on y; PowerBasis.algHom_ext proves uniqueness. Apply the homomorphism to every marked equality, using preservation of polynomial evaluation and division.

<a id="target-arithmeticdynamics-dy-6-followup-benedetto-zero-height"></a>

### 6.53 Benedetto zero-height criterion for nonisotrivial polynomials

Let F be any field, K/F a finite extension of F(T), and f∈K[z] a polynomial of degree d≥2 which is not affine-conjugate over a finite extension of K to a polynomial over the algebraic constant field. For every x∈P¹(K̄), its geometric canonical height is zero if and only if x is preperiodic.

The height uses geometric places trivial on F; this is not the number-field Northcott argument. Isotriviality allows a finite extension and an affine change of coordinates.

Over any fixed finite extension containing x, zero local escape rates place its forward orbit in every local filled Julia set. The rational zero-height set is forward-invariant. If it has at most two points it is already finite. Otherwise, if all places have potentially good reduction, normalize two finite zero-height points to 0 and 1; the product formula forces the leading coefficient to have norm 1 everywhere and then forces all coefficients to be constants (Benedetto Proposition 6.1). Nonisotriviality therefore supplies a bad place in this remaining case. At a bad place the filled Julia set is covered by at most d² open discs of radius |a_d|^{-1/(d−1)}; at good places it lies in a closed disc of that radius. Two rational points in the same choices of bad-place discs violate the product formula. Thus the rational zero-height set is finite and forward-invariant. Apply this argument in a finite extension containing any algebraic x. Nonisotriviality persists under that extension.

### 6.54 Composition of Lattès maps: f_{E,m} ∘ f_{E,n} = f_{E,mn}

Let F be a field, E/F a Weierstrass curve with Δ(E) ≠ 0 and m, n nonzero integers. Then f_{E,m} ∘ f_{E,n} = f_{E,mn} as rational maps of ℙ¹_F (equality of the composite pair of forms with (Φ_{mn}^h, ΨSq_{mn}^h) up to a scalar in F^×). In particular f_{E,n}^k = f_{E,n^k}.

Δ(E) ≠ 0; m, n ≠ 0.

In the function field F(E), the pullback of x along [n] is Φ_n(x)/ΨSq_n(x) (TauCeti.Isogeny.fieldPullback_mulByIntIsogeny_X), and [m] ∘ [n] = [mn] as isogenies (TauCeti.Isogeny.mulByIntIsogeny_comp_mulByIntIsogeny), whose field pullbacks compose (TauCeti.Isogeny.comp_fieldPullback). Pulling x back along [mn] in the two ways gives the identity Φ_m(r)/ΨSq_m(r) = Φ_{mn}(x)/ΨSq_{mn}(x) in F(E), with r = Φ_n(x)/ΨSq_n(x); since F(x) → F(E) is injective, it holds in F(x) = RatFunc F. Two coprime pairs of forms of degree D that define the same rational function are proportional (clear denominators and use coprimality); the composite forms of f_{E,m} ∘ f_{E,n} have degree m²n² = deg f_{E,mn} (DY.0 composition of forms), so the two rational maps coincide. Alternative check on points: over an algebraic closure every a is an x-coordinate (WeierstrassCurve.Affine.exists_point_on_curve), and f_{E,m}(f_{E,n}(x(P))) = x(m(nP)) = f_{E,mn}(x(P)) (DY.6/lattes-map-semiconjugacy); two rational maps agreeing at infinitely many points are equal (Polynomial.eq_zero_of_infinite_isRoot applied to the cross-multiplied difference).

### 6.55 Flexible Lattès maps and the flexible Lattès locus

Let K be a field of characteristic 0 with algebraic closure K̄, and d ≥ 2. A rational map f of degree d over K is a flexible Lattès map if there exist an elliptic Weierstrass curve E over K̄, an integer n with |n| ≥ 2, a point T ∈ E(K̄) with 2T = O, and a Möbius transformation φ ∈ PGL₂(K̄) such that φ ∘ f ∘ φ⁻¹ = τ_T ∘ f_{E,n} over K̄ (DY.6/two-torsion-translation, τ_O = id), i.e. f is conjugate to the descent of P ↦ nP + T through x. Then d = n². The flexible Lattès locus L_d ⊂ M_d(K̄) (DY.0/moduli-space-of-rational-maps) is the set of conjugacy classes of flexible Lattès maps of degree d; it is empty unless d is a perfect square.

char K = 0 (the sources work over ℂ and ℚ̄; the translation τ_T needs char ≠ 2). The Möbius transformation and the curve may be defined only over K̄. Rigid Lattès maps (quotients of complex-multiplication endomorphisms, or by the groups of order 3, 4, 6) are not flexible and are not constructed in DY.6.

x(nP + T) = τ_T(x(nP)) = τ_T(f_{E,n}(x(P))) (DY.6/two-torsion-translation, DY.6/lattes-map-semiconjugacy), so τ_T ∘ f_{E,n} is the descent of P ↦ nP + T; its degree is n² since τ_T is Möbius. The predicate is invariant under conjugation by PGL₂(K̄) by construction, so it descends to conjugacy classes (DY.0/conjugacy-of-rational-maps) and defines L_d ⊆ M_d(K̄). Milnor's Lemma 5.5: a Lattès map is flexible iff it is a quotient by ±1 of τ ↦ aτ + b with a ∈ ℤ; commuting with −1 forces 2b ∈ Λ, so b is a 2-torsion point and the map is τ_b ∘ f_{E,a} with E(ℂ) = ℂ/Λ.

### 6.56 The symmetries t ↦ 1 − t and t ↦ 1/t of the Legendre Lattès family

For a field F of characteristic ≠ 2 and t ∈ F ∖ {0, 1}, with A(z, w) = (w − z, w) and B(z, w) = (z, tw): A ∘ F_t = −F_{1−t} ∘ A and B ∘ F_t = F_{1/t} ∘ B as maps F² → F², and more generally A ∘ F_tⁿ = −F_{1−t}ⁿ ∘ A and B ∘ F_tⁿ = F_{1/t}ⁿ ∘ B for all n ≥ 1. On ℙ¹: f_{1−t} = α ∘ f_t ∘ α⁻¹ with α(z) = 1 − z, and f_{1/t} = β ∘ f_t ∘ β⁻¹ with β(z) = z/t.

char F ≠ 2; t ≠ 0, 1.

Second coordinates: the second coordinate of F_{1−t}(A(z, w)) is 4(w − z)w(−z)(tw − z) = −4zw(z − w)(z − tw), the negative of the second coordinate of F_t(z, w); first coordinates: (z² − 2zw + tw²)² − (z² − tw²)² = −4zw(z − w)(z − tw), so G − F = −(z² − 2zw + tw²)² with (F, G) = F_t(z, w); this is A ∘ F_t = −F_{1−t} ∘ A (a polynomial identity, ring). ### 6.58 Standard projections of an elliptic curve

Let E be an elliptic curve over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic ≠2. A standard projection is π=φ∘x for φ∈PGL₂(k), where x(O)=∞. Equivalently it is a degree-two quotient identifying P and −P, followed by a projective coordinate choice. Translating by any e∈E[2] gives another map of this form because x∘τ_e=ι_e∘x for a Möbius map ι_e. The branch set π(E[2]) has four points, and π(E^tors)=φ(x(E^tors)); precomposing by τ_e leaves the torsion-image set unchanged.

k algebraically closed, char k ≠ 2. Over ℂ these are exactly the degree-two quotients π with π(P) = π(−P) composed with 2-torsion translations.

x ∘ τ_e(P) = τ_e-image of x(P) (DY.6/two-torsion-translation), so π is φ ∘ τ_e′ ∘ x with τ_e′ a Möbius map; it identifies Q and −Q + 2e = −Q. Branch set: x is ramified exactly at E[2] (x(P) = x(−P), P = −P iff P ∈ E[2]), so π(E[2]) = φ(τ_e(x(E[2]))) has four points. π(E^tors) = φ(τ_e(x(E^tors))) = φ(x(E^tors + e)) = φ(x(E^tors)) since E^tors + e = E^tors.

The reusable interface consists of the following statements.

- **`standardProjection`** (constructor): π=φ∘x for φ∈PGL₂(k); the alternative φ∘x∘τ_e with e∈E[2] is obtained by absorbing ι_e into the Möbius parameter.
- **`standardProjection_neg`** (characterisation): π(−P + 2e) = π(P), i.e. π(−P) = π(P) for e ∈ E[2] (2e = O).
- **`standardProjection_branchSet`** (characterisation): The points of ℙ¹ with exactly one preimage under π are the four points of π(E[2]); π is two-to-one elsewhere.
- **`standardProjection_torsion`** (relation): π(E^tors) = φ(x(E^tors)).
- **`standardProjection_normalize`** (other): A Möbius transformation ψ moves the branch set π(E[2]) to {0, 1, t, ∞} for some t ≠ 0, 1; after translating by a 2-torsion point so that π(O) = ∞, E is in Legendre form E_t.

**Checks.**

- **`standardProjection_legendre`** (computation): For E_t and e = O, φ = id, the standard projection is x, with branch set {0, 1, t, ∞}.
- **`standardProjection_translate`** (degenerate): Translating by e ∈ E[2] does not change the set of torsion images: π^e(E^tors) = π(E^tors).
- **`standardProjection_branch_card`** (compatibility): The branch set π(E[2]) has exactly four points (the roots of Ψ₂Sq and ∞ for π = x, Mathlib WeierstrassCurve.Ψ₂Sq).
- **`standardProjection_not_three_to_one`** (non-example): The map E → ℙ¹ given by the y-coordinate of y² = x³ + 1 has degree 3, is not a quotient by P ↦ −P, and is not a standard projection.

**Endpoint checks.** For E_t, x itself is a standard projection with branch set {0, 1, t, ∞}.

### 6.61 A birational height comparison (DeMarco–Krieger–Ye Lemma 6.3)

t₁ ≠ t₂, both ≠ 0, 1.

g(x₁, x₂) = (x₂/x₁, (1 − x₂)/(1 − x₁)) is birational on ℙ² with inverse g⁻¹(y₁, y₂) = ((1 − y₂)/(y₁ − y₂), y₁(1 − y₂)/(y₁ − y₂)), a degree-2 map with indeterminacy {(0 : 1 : 0), (1 : 0 : 0), (1 : 1 : 1)}. Heights under rational maps: off the indeterminacy locus, h(g⁻¹(P)) ≤ 2h(P) + C (Mathlib Height.logHeight_eval_le for the three quadratic forms of g⁻¹, in the absolute normalisation of DY.6/absolute-height-bounds-for-forms (a)); the points (t₂/t₁, (1 − t₂)/(1 − t₁)) avoid the indeterminacy for t₁ ≠ t₂ in ℚ̄ ∖ {0, 1}. Apply with P = g(t₁, t₂), so g⁻¹(P) = (t₁, t₂).

### 6.62 An unramified map returns to the residue class to first order (Bell–Ghioca–Tucker Propositions 2.4 and 2.6)

In the setting of DY.6/p-adic-power-series-coordinates, write F(β⃗) = C⃗ + L β⃗ + (higher order terms). If Φ is unramified at x, then L is invertible modulo p, and there is n ≥ 1 with Fⁿ(β⃗) ≡ β⃗ (mod p) for all β⃗ ∈ ℤ_p^g.

### 6.63 Simple-root primes for a family with prescribed denominator exclusions

Let n ≥ 0, R = ℤ[T₁,…,Tₙ], and H ∈ R[Y] have positive natural degree and separable image in (FractionRing R)[Y]. Let D be a finite set of nonzero parameter polynomials. For every N ∈ ℕ there exist a ∈ ℤⁿ, a prime p > N and b ∈ ℤ such that Hₐ = H(Y,a) has the same natural degree as H, p ∤ lc(H)(a), p ∤ q(a) for all q ∈ D, p ∣ Hₐ(b), and p ∤ Hₐ′(b).

The prime and integral parameter specialization are chosen together; the conclusion does not apply to every prime or every specialization. No algebraic independence of a is asserted: a is only the integral residue-box centre for the later p-adic perturbation. Nonconstant H is essential; p = 2 is not forbidden here, while N = 3 forces p ≥ 5 when the analytic consumer needs it.

Apply DY.6/lech-integral-specialization-certificate to obtain A,B,c,a with c(a), lc(H)(a) and all q(a) nonzero, and the degree equality. Set m = lc(H)(a)·∏q∈D q(a), a nonzero integer (empty product one). Map AH + BH′ = C c along evaluation at a; Polynomial.derivative_map gives the exact derivative required by DY.6/simple-root-prime-avoiding. Apply that existing prime-selection node to Hₐ, Aₐ, Bₐ, c(a), m and N. It gives p > N with p ∤ m and a simple residue root b. Each excluded factor divides m, so p divides neither lc(H)(a) nor any q(a). No Chebotarev or Hilbert irreducibility is used. The output is the exact residue data consumed by the remaining algebraically independent p-adic perturbation and Hensel steps of DY.6/lech-embedding-lemma. Producing H and D from the original field, and extending the eventual root to a field embedding, remain separate gaps.

<a id="target-arithmeticdynamics-dy-6-lattes-map-preperiodic-iff-torsion"></a>

### 6.64 Preperiodic points of a Lattès map are the torsion images

Let F be a field, E/F a Weierstrass curve with Δ(E) ≠ 0 and n ∈ ℤ with |n| ≥ 2. For P ∈ E(F), the point x(P) ∈ ℙ¹(F) is preperiodic for f_{E,n} if and only if P has finite order. If F is algebraically closed, the set of preperiodic points of f_{E,n} in ℙ¹(F) is exactly x(E(F)_tors) (which contains ∞ = x(O)).

Δ(E) ≠ 0; |n| ≥ 2; no characteristic hypothesis.

By DY.6/lattes-map-semiconjugacy and DY.6/lattes-map-comp, f_{E,n}^k(x(P)) = x(n^k P) for all k. If P has finite order N, the points n^k P lie in the finite group generated by P, so the forward orbit of x(P) is finite. Conversely, if f^a(x(P)) = f^b(x(P)) with a < b, then x(n^a P) = x(n^b P). Points with the same x-coordinate are equal or opposite (WeierstrassCurve.Affine.Y_eq_of_X_eq for affine points; only O has x = ∞), so n^b P = ±n^a P and (n^b ∓ n^a)P = O with n^b ∓ n^a ≠ 0 because |n^b| > |n^a|; hence P has finite order (the additive form of isOfFinOrder_iff_pow_eq_one). Over an algebraically closed F, every a ∈ F is x(P) for some P (WeierstrassCurve.Affine.exists_point_on_curve, nonsingular by WeierstrassCurve.Affine.equation_iff_nonsingular_of_Δ_ne_zero), which gives the description of all preperiodic points.

### 6.65 The canonical height of a Lattès map is twice the Néron–Tate height

Let K be a number field, E/K a Weierstrass curve with Δ(E) ≠ 0, n ∈ ℤ with |n| ≥ 2, and P ∈ E(K). Let ĥ_{f_{E,n}} be the canonical height of f_{E,n} on ℙ¹(ℚ̄) normalised against the absolute Weil height (DY.1/canonical-height-on-the-projective-line), and canonicalHeight the Néron–Tate height of Tau Ceti (WeierstrassCurve.Affine.Point.canonicalHeight: ½ lim h_K(x(2^kP))/4^k with the height h_K relative to K, normalised to the divisor (O)). Then ĥ_{f_{E,n}}(x(P)) = 2 · canonicalHeight(P)/[K : ℚ], independently of n. In absolute normalisation this is DeMarco–Krieger–Ye's ĥ_E(P) = ½ ĥ_f(x(P)). More generally, for any field F with an admissible family of absolute values, the relative height satisfies ĥ^F_{f_{E,n}}(x(P)) = 2ĥ_E(P), using Tau Ceti’s relative Néron–Tate height. The number-field formula follows by dividing by [F:ℚ].

K a number field (Mathlib NumberField.instAdmissibleAbsValues); E elliptic; |n| ≥ 2. For the relative version, F is any admissible global height field; the elliptic curve is nonsingular and |n| ≥ 2. No Northcott assumption is needed for this identity.

The naive height is naiveHeight(Q) = logHeight₁(x(Q)) relative to K (WeierstrassCurve.Affine.Point.naiveHeight_eq_logHeight₁), and absLogHeight₁(a) = logHeight₁(a)/[K : ℚ] for a ∈ K (DiophantineApproximationAndTranscendence:DT.0/abs-mul-height-eq-rpow). f_{E,n}^k(x(P)) = x(n^k P) (DY.6/lattes-map-semiconjugacy, DY.6/lattes-map-comp), so ĥ_{f_{E,n}}(x(P)) = lim_k naiveHeight(n^k P)/(n^{2k}[K : ℚ]) by the defining limit of DY.1/canonical-height-on-the-projective-line. canonicalHeight(n^k P) = n^{2k} canonicalHeight(P) (WeierstrassCurve.Affine.Point.canonicalHeight_zsmul) and |canonicalHeight(Q) − naiveHeight(Q)/2| ≤ D for all Q (WeierstrassCurve.Affine.Point.abs_canonicalHeight_sub_naiveHeight_le); dividing by n^{2k} and letting k → ∞ gives naiveHeight(n^k P)/n^{2k} → 2 canonicalHeight(P).

### 6.66 Flexible Lattès maps are postcritically finite

Let K be an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0, E/K elliptic, |n| ≥ 2, T ∈ E[2] and g = τ_T ∘ f_{E,n}. Every critical point of g (DY.0/critical-points-of-a-rational-map) is x(P) for some P with nP ∈ E[2], and g(x(E[2])) ⊆ x(E[2]). Hence the postcritical set of g is contained in the four points x(E[2]) = {∞} ∪ {roots of Ψ₂Sq}, g is postcritically finite (DY.6/postcritically-finite-map), and so is every flexible Lattès map. Precisely, the critical points of f_{E,n} are the 2n² − 2 points x(P) with nP ∈ E[2] and P ∉ E[2], each of multiplicity one.

char K = 0 (so that [n] is separable and τ_T is defined); K algebraically closed.

Invariant differential: [n]*ω = n ω for ω = dx/η, η = 2y + a₁x + a₃ (TauCeti.Isogeny.pullbackDifferential_mulByIntIsogeny_invariantDifferential), and the pullback of x along [n] is f_{E,n}(x) (TauCeti.Isogeny.fieldPullback_mulByIntIsogeny_X). Comparing the two sides gives f_{E,n}′(x) · η = n · (η ∘ [n]) in K(E). Evaluating at an affine P with nP affine and P ∉ E[2] (both sides regular; η(P) ≠ 0): f_{E,n}′(x(P)) = n η(nP)/η(P), which vanishes iff η(nP) = 0 iff nP ∈ E[2]. If P ∈ E[2] then nP ∈ E[2] anyway. The poles x(P) with nP = O also satisfy nP ∈ E[2]. So every critical point c = x(P) has nP ∈ E[2], and g(c) = x(nP + T) ∈ x(E[2]). x(E[2]) is forward invariant: g(x(Q)) = x(nQ + T) with nQ + T ∈ E[2] for Q ∈ E[2]. Counting (for the multiplicities): #[n]⁻¹(E[2]) = 4n², of which the 4 points of E[2] are not critical (the local degrees satisfy e_f(x(P))·e_x(P) = e_x(nP) with e_x = 2 exactly on E[2]), leaving 4n² − 4 points and 2n² − 2 = 2 deg g − 2 simple critical points. Conjugation by φ preserves postcritical finiteness, giving the statement for every flexible Lattès map.

### 6.67 Affine-torus Lattès maps

A complex rational map f of degree ≥2 is an affine-torus Lattès map if there exist a rank-two lattice Λ⊂C, the torus T=C/Λ, an affine endomorphism L(z)=az+b with aΛ⊂Λ and |a|²>1, and a finite holomorphic quotient Θ:T→P¹ such that f∘Θ=Θ∘L. The classification normalizes Θ to T/G_n for n∈{2,3,4,6}, with ω_nΛ=Λ and (1−ω_n)b∈Λ. Flexibility is equivalent to n=2 and a an integer.

Λ has rank two; cylinder quotients give power/Chebyshev maps and are excluded. Finite quotient is essential. The translation b is allowed; the inherited multiplication-only Lattès map is a special case.

Use the quotient-of-affine-map notion of Milnor Definition 2.1 restricted to a torus. The semiconjugacy determines degree |a|². Milnor Theorem 3.1 and Lemma 3.5 give the cyclic quotient normal form; Theorem 5.1 fixes the conjugacy invariants. Lemma 5.5 identifies flexibility. Elliptic uniformization and the cyclic-quotient classification remain a precise recorded gap; do not identify the whole notion with inherited multiplication-only maps.
